column1: # Live RBAC route matrix: Phase 2 (identity). Each step adds the rows of the behaviour it
# changes; a row of an earlier file whose answer a step changes is tagged superseded-by:p2 there.
# Columns: id, since, actor, method, path, body, expect, tags (see tests/rbac_matrix_live.sh).
# ---- step 2.2: the session version in the login token ----
# member_a and admin_a sign in; the runner raises the account's session version by SQL just
# before each *_revoked row and puts it back right after (the cookie kept), so the row sends a
# login cookie of an older version. With the identity switch on the refusal clears the cookie
# on its own 401 (an expired redamon-auth in the answer's headers) and /api/auth/me says
# session_ended (the browser goes to /login); off, both stay as after Phase 1. Each control
# sends the same request with the cookie of the current version. POST /api/users answers a missing session with 403 and refuses an
# empty body after its admin check (400), so no account is ever created.
# ---- step 2.3: account status: disable, enable, sign out everywhere ----
# No row changes an account: each sends what the route refuses after its checks (another
# admin's account, the own account, an unknown id, a body that is not JSON), or enables an
# account that is already active (200 "changed":false). With the identity switch off disable,
# revoke-sessions and revoke-all do not exist (404 before any check) and enable stays open.
# The stateful flow (disable, the old cookie and the sign-in refused, enable, revoke) is
# ---- step 2.4: instance settings (the tunnel and the TrafficMind capture policy) ----
# With the identity switch on they live in the instance settings: GET/PUT
# /api/admin/instance-settings as the signed-in person (an admin; the tunnel also the
# `tunnels` legacy holder, none seeded here), and the user settings PUT refuses a real change
# of one with 409 before anything is written. Off, the route does not exist (404) and the
# p1 tunnel rows hold. No row writes: the PUTs are refused before the row is read or written
# (not JSON 415, a tunnel field that is not text 400, a member 403, a moved field 409). Since
# step 3.9 a member holding neither field group (no tunnel, no capture) and no administrator
# account is refused naming platform:tunnels, with the permissions switch on or off
# (instance:settings is Root's security policy, not this gate). The
# tunnel sync takes only the sandbox's bearer whatever the switch (the accepted call:
# ---- step 2.6: only Root manages admins; the security policy; the Root transfer ----
# rbac-admin-a is an admin, never Root (on the dev stack Root is the owner's own account), so with
# the identity switch on every action on rbac-admin-b, a promotion or an admin creation answers
# 403 root_only before any password is checked: nothing is created or changed, and the rows that
# carry the right password prove it is never even tried. The p1 step-up rows of the same requests
# run only with the switch off. The transfer routes do not exist with the switch off (404); on, an
# admin that is not Root offers nothing, and with no offer pending accept and cancel answer 409
# before any password. The stateful flows (Root's own powers, a transfer, decline and cancel) run
# With the identity switch on every new password meets the policy in force (the instance minimum,
# the deny list, not the account's email, not one repeated character). Each row is refused after
# the authorization check, so nothing changes; with the switch off the same requests would set the
# password, so they run only with it on. Off, the policy route answers 404.
# ---- step 2.9: invite links and the public invite page ----
# The admin routes exist only with the identity switch on. Each "allowed" row is refused after the
# authorization check (a bad body, an address in use, an account that is not invited), so no account
# or link is made. The public paths are reached with no cookie; with the switch off they are like
# any unknown path (sign-in redirect, 401). The unknown-link row costs one lookup of the per-copy
# No row resets an account: each sends what the route refuses after its checks (a member, the
# own account, another admin without Root's power, a mode that does not exist, an unknown id, a
# temporary password the policy refuses once the reason is given). With the identity switch off
# the route does not exist (404 before any check). The stateful flow (a reset link with a reason,
# the open session ended, the link used, the notice shown once, one auth.login.after_reset row) is
# ---- step 2.11: email change, session lifetimes, My activity ----
# With the identity switch on, changing a sign-in email takes the current password (own) or the
# admin's own (a member's): without it 403 step_up_required before anything is read or written.
# An address another account holds in other capitals is 409 email_taken, answered only after the
# password (rbac-member-b gives its right password, rbac-admin-a its own for member B's address, so
# nothing is written either way); off, Phase 1 answers the collision without a password
# (p2-email-taken-off, p1-email-edit-collision). The login cookie lives as long as its token: an admin
# 12 h, a member 168 h with the switch on (the instance row's defaults, PLACEHOLDER(OQ-38): these rows
# assume Root left them), 7 days for everyone off. My activity is the signed-in account's, 404 off.
# The stateful flow (an email change with the password, its notice and activity row, an idle admin
# sent to sign-in) is E2E-P2-09, tests/rbac_account_live.sh on a disposable instance.
# ---- step 2.12: same-origin JSON on the identity routes ----
# Each row is a page of another site (origin:https://rbac-other-site.example) sending what the route
# would refuse after its checks anyway (an empty body, the own account, an unknown token, a value
# that is not valid), so a missing origin check changes nothing: it only answers that refusal
# instead of 403 cross_origin. The Phase 1 routes check the origin whatever the identity switch (a
# security fix); the Phase 2 routes answer 404 first with the switch off, so their rows run on only.
# The control row is the same request from the webapp's own origin (what the app sends), refused
# for its body after the check. The public invite form checks it too (anon, no session).
